questions.title: Products with no colour
questions.story: The product team wants to see how many products there are in each colour. Products with a missing colour should show as 'Unknown'. Return the colour and the number of products.

questions.title: Fix the typos in the account list

questions.title: Deals lost in a join
questions.story: In Combining Data you listed the 2017 won deals priced above the list price and got 1,674. For won deals closed in 2017, return three numbers: how many deals there are, how many found a list price, and how many closed above the list price.
questions.hint: Use REPLACE(product, 'GTXPro', 'GTX Pro') in the join condition. After the fix, the number of deals that found a price should equal the number of won deals.

questions.title: Customers by age group

questions.title: Repeated customer names
questions.story: The data team thinks GBE_Customers contains duplicate customers, because 15,266 customers have only 15,118 different names. Check it. For each name that appears more than once, return the name, how many times it is listed, and how many different birthdays it has.

questions.title: Orders far above average
questions.story: Finance wants to review unusually large orders before the monthly report. Flag an order as an outlier when its TotalDue is more than 2 standard deviations above the average TotalDue of all orders. Return how many orders are flagged and how many orders there are in total.
questions.hint: STDEV(TotalDue) gives the standard deviation. Calculate the average and STDEV in a CTE or subquery, then compare each order with average + 2 x STDEV.

questions.title: Two ways to find outliers
questions.story: Repeat the outlier check with the IQR rule. An order is an outlier when TotalDue is above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR, where IQR = Q3 - Q1. Compare the number of flagged orders with the standard deviation method from the last question. Which method flags more orders, and why? Would you remove these orders? Write your conclusion below.
questions.hint: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY TotalDue) OVER () gives Q1. Use 0.75 for Q3.

questions.title: Validate the cleaned accounts
questions.story: Before you share the cleaned account list from the typo question, validate it. Return one row with four numbers: the total number of rows, the number of different accounts, the rows where the sector is still 'technolgy', and the rows where the office location is still 'Philipines'.
questions.hint: Rebuild the cleaned list in a CTE, then count on top of it. The validation must run on the cleaned data, not on CRM_Accounts.

questions.title: R, F and M for every customer
questions.story: Marketing wants to segment customers by how recently, how often and how much they buy. Start with the raw numbers. For every customer in ADW_Sales_orders, return Recency (days between the customer's last order and 2014-07-01), Frequency (number of orders) and Monetary (total TotalDue).
questions.hint: DATEDIFF(day, MAX(OrderDate), '2014-07-01'), COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) and SUM(TotalDue), all grouped by CustomerID.

questions.title: Score each customer from 1 to 5
questions.story: Turn the three numbers into scores. For each customer, calculate PERCENT_RANK for Recency, Frequency and Monetary, then cut each percentile into five bands: up to 0.2 is 1, up to 0.4 is 2, up to 0.6 is 3, up to 0.8 is 4, and above 0.8 is 5. A recent customer must get a high Recency score, so rank Recency from the most days to the fewest (ORDER BY Recency DESC). Return CustomerID, R_score, F_score and M_score.
questions.hint: Put the R, F and M calculation from the last question in a CTE. Then use three PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ...) columns and a CASE WHEN for each band.

questions.title: Size and value of each segment
questions.story:
Marketing needs a simple segment list. Using the scores from the last question, put each customer in the first segment they match:
- Champions: R, F and M scores are all 4 or 5.
- Loyal: F score is 4 or 5.
- Promising: R score is 4 or 5.
- At Risk: M score is 4 or 5.
- Hibernating: everyone else.
For each segment, return the number of customers, the number of orders and the total revenue (TotalDue).
questions.hint: A CASE WHEN checks the conditions from top to bottom, and the first true one wins. Join the segments back to ADW_Sales_orders on CustomerID to count orders and add up revenue.

questions.title: How each segment buys
questions.story: The CRM team asks if there is any notable buying behaviour in each segment. For each segment from the last question, return the average order value (AOV), the number of orders per customer and the share of orders placed online. Then write two findings and one action for the team.
questions.hint: AOV = total TotalDue divided by the number of orders. The online share uses OnlineOrderFlag, which is 1 for online orders.
questions.note: Champions AOV 11,035; At Risk 2,652; Loyal 2,509; Promising 606; Hibernating 230

questions.title: Favourite category of each segment
questions.story: Which product category brings the most revenue in each segment? Return the segment, the category, the revenue (LineTotal) and the category's share of the segment's revenue, ranked within each segment. Does any segment buy differently from the others?
questions.hint: Join the segments to the orders, the order lines, the products, the sub-categories and the categories. Use SUM(LineTotal) OVER (PARTITION BY segment) for the share.

questions.title: First purchase month
questions.story: Retention analysis starts by putting each customer in a cohort, which is the month of their first order. For every customer in ADW_Sales_orders, return the CustomerID and the CohortMonth: the first day of the month of the customer's first OrderDate.
questions.hint: MIN(OrderDate) per customer gives the first order. DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(x), MONTH(x), 1) turns a date into the first day of its month.

questions.title: Cohort sizes
questions.story: How many new customers does each monthly cohort have? Return the CohortMonth and the number of customers.
questions.hint: Use the query from the last question as a CTE, then COUNT(*) grouped by CohortMonth.

questions.title: Active customers by month since first order
questions.story: For each cohort, count the customers who ordered in each month after their first. Return the CohortMonth, MonthsSinceFirst (0 for the first month) and the number of different active customers.
questions.hint: List the months in which each customer ordered (DISTINCT customer and month), join it to the first order month, and use DATEDIFF(month, cohort month, order month).

questions.title: Cohort table, months 0 to 3
questions.story: Reshape the last result into a cohort table: one row per cohort with four columns, month0, month1, month2 and month3. Each column holds the number of different customers who ordered that many months after their first order.
questions.hint: Conditional aggregation: COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN MonthsSinceFirst = 1 THEN CustomerID END) for each column.

questions.title: Retention rates and what they show
questions.story: Add the retention rate to the cohort table. Return the CohortMonth, the cohort size and the retention rate for months 1, 2 and 3 as a percent of the cohort size, rounded to 1 decimal. The data ends on 2014-06-30, so a month that has not happened yet must show NULL, not 0. Then answer: for each cohort, is there anything special?
questions.hint: Retention rate = active customers in that month / cohort size (month0). Show a rate only when the cohort month plus the number of months is on or before 2014-06-01, otherwise leave the CASE without an ELSE.

questions.title: Two win rates
questions.story: The Sales Director says the win rate looks low. Before you analyse anything, fix the definition. Return the number of closed deals (stage Won or Lost), the number of won deals, the win rate as a percent of closed deals and the win rate as a percent of all deals in the pipeline, both rounded to 1 decimal. Then write the metric line of your analytics question: which rate would you use, and why?
questions.hint: A closed deal has the stage Won or Lost. Engaging and Prospecting deals are still open: they sit in the second denominator but not in the first.

questions.title: Which split covers every deal?
questions.story: You plan three branches for an issue tree on the pipeline: by sales team (join to CRM_sales_teams on the agent), by account sector (join to CRM_Accounts on the account) and by product list (join to CRM_products on the product name). A branch is only useful if it reaches every deal. For each split, return the split name, the number of deals it reaches and the number of deals it misses, out of all deals in CRM_sales_pipeline. Which branches are collectively exhaustive?
questions.hint: Count the rows after each inner join and subtract from the total number of deals in the pipeline.

questions.title: Win rate by quarter, and the months behind it
questions.story: The Director says: "The win rate was great in the first quarter and has been lower since." For each quarter of 2017 (by close date), return how many different months of closed deals it holds, the number of closed deals and the win rate (percent of closed deals, 1 decimal). Count only closed deals. Can the first quarter be compared with the others?
questions.hint: Use CASE WHEN on MONTH(close_date) to build the quarter. T-SQL does not let you reuse the SELECT alias in GROUP BY, so repeat the CASE or build it in a CTE.

questions.title: Is the March jump the same in every office?
questions.story: An issue tree for "why is the win rate different in March?" has a segment branch (who sells) and a time branch (when deals close). Test the segment branch. For each regional office (CRM_sales_teams, joined on the agent), return the win rate in March and the win rate from April to December, both as a percent of closed deals rounded to 1 decimal. Does the gap come from one office?
questions.hint: Two conditional aggregations per office: one for March, one for the months after. Divide each by the closed deals of the same period, not by all closed deals.

questions.title: AdventureWorks channels in numbers
questions.story: You have been asked to research AdventureWorks before an analysis. Fill the channel and revenue blocks of a Business Model Canvas with data. An order is online when OnlineOrderFlag = 1 and sold by a sales rep otherwise. For each channel, return the number of orders, its percent of all orders, the revenue (sum of SubTotal), its percent of revenue and the average order value (revenue divided by orders). Round percents to 1 decimal and the average to 0 decimals.
questions.hint: A window over an aggregate gives the percent of total: SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () is the total number of orders.

questions.title: Orders by sales reason: overlap and gap
questions.story: A colleague wants to break orders down by sales reason (ADW_Sales_orders_reasons, one row per order and reason). Before the chart, test the breakdown. Return the total number of orders, the number of rows in the reasons table, the number of orders that have at least one reason, the number of orders with no reason and the number of orders with two or more reasons. Is "orders by sales reason" MECE?
questions.hint: Four small subqueries. Use COUNT(DISTINCT SalesOrderID) for the orders that have a reason, and GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 for the orders with several.

questions.title: Split won value into input metrics
questions.story: Won value is an output metric. The Sales Director wants the input metrics behind it. For each product, among closed deals, return the number of closed deals, the win rate (percent, 1 decimal), the average value of a won deal (0 decimals) and the total won value. Then compare GTXPro with GTX Basic: they win about the same share of deals, yet GTXPro earns far more. Which input metric explains it?
questions.hint: Won value = closed deals x win rate x average won value. Compute the three inputs and the output in one grouped query.

questions.title: Does the detail follow the total?
questions.story: Revenue (sum of LineTotal) grew between 2012 and 2013. Does every category grow at the same pace? Return one row per category plus a row called 'All categories', with the revenue in 2012, the revenue in 2013 (0 decimals) and the growth in percent (1 decimal).
questions.hint: Build one CTE with category, year and line total for 2012 and 2013, then aggregate it twice: by category, and for the total row. Join the lines to the order header for the date and walk the product chain for the category.

questions.title: How many groups does each dimension return?
questions.story: Before you group, guess how many rows come back. Check your guesses. Return the number of groups for each of these dimensions, one row per dimension with the columns dimension and groups: product category, product sub-category, product sold (in the order lines), sales territory, customer (in the orders) and year-month of the order. Which of them are a dimension, and which is a key?
questions.hint: COUNT(DISTINCT column) per dimension, stacked with UNION ALL. For the year-month, count distinct YEAR(OrderDate) * 100 + MONTH(OrderDate).

questions.title: The 80/20 check by sub-category
questions.story: Work where the mass is. Rank the product sub-categories by revenue (sum of LineTotal, 0 decimals). Return the sub-category, its revenue, its percent of total revenue and the cumulative percent (both 1 decimal), from the largest to the smallest. How many sub-categories make up 80% of revenue?
questions.hint: A running total needs a window: SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC). Divide by SUM(revenue) OVER () for the share of the total.

questions.title: Where did first-half growth come from?
questions.story: Compare the first half of 2014 (January to June) with the first half of 2013 by sales territory, using the sum of SubTotal. Return the territory, the revenue in each period, the change, and each territory's share of the total change (percent, 1 decimal). Which territory contributes most, and is the total moving in the same direction as its biggest parts?
questions.hint: Aggregate revenue per territory for each half-year with conditional SUMs, then use a window SUM over the changes for the share of the total change.

questions.title: A discount on online clothing
questions.story: Marketing proposes a 10% price cut on all Clothing sold online. Use 2013 as the base. Return one row with the revenue (sum of LineTotal), the cost (sum of OrderQty x StandardCost from ADW_Dim_Product), the gross profit, and the unit lift in percent (1 decimal) that the discount needs to leave gross profit unchanged. Round money to 0 decimals. Would you recommend it?
questions.hint: After a 10% price cut, revenue per unit is 0.9 times the old value and cost per unit is unchanged. Break-even lift = (old gross profit) / (new gross profit per base unit) - 1.

questions.title: Leader by total, leader by rate
questions.story: A slide will rank products by won value. Check whether the ranking changes when you use the win rate. For each product, among closed deals, return the total won value, the win rate (percent, 1 decimal), the rank by won value and the rank by win rate (rank 1 is the highest). Which product would you put first on a slide about sales efficiency?
questions.hint: Compute won value and the win rate in a CTE, then add two RANK() OVER columns with different ORDER BY.

questions.title: Top 3 categories and Other
questions.story: A chart of units sold by product category has eight bars. Make it readable for a slide. Return the three categories that sold the most units, plus one row called 'Other' for all the rest. Show the units and the percent of all units (1 decimal). Put the three categories first, from largest to smallest, and 'Other' last.
questions.hint: Units per category first, rank them, then relabel everything below rank 3 as 'Other' and add up again.

questions.title: Mean or median order value?
questions.story: The report says "the average order value in 2013 was X". For each channel (online, sales rep), return the number of orders placed in 2013, the mean SubTotal and the median SubTotal (0 decimals). If they disagree, which one would you put on the slide?
questions.hint: The median is the middle row when orders are sorted. Number the rows per channel with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY SubTotal), count the rows per channel, and average the one or two middle rows (rn * 2 IN (n, n + 1, n + 2)).

questions.title: Winners only: who is missing?
questions.story: A slide says "the average deal is worth X" for each product. Check what the average covers. For each product, return the average value of won deals (0 decimals) and the average value across all closed deals, counting a lost deal at its stored value (0 decimals). What does the first number leave out?
questions.hint: AVG ignores NULL, so AVG(CASE WHEN deal_stage = 'Won' THEN close_value END) averages the won deals only. A plain AVG(close_value) over the closed deals includes the lost ones.

questions.title: Two headlines for 2014
questions.story: The data ends on 2014-06-30. For each product category, return two numbers: the revenue (sum of LineTotal) change in percent (1 decimal) from full-year 2013 to full-year 2014, and the change from January-June 2013 to January-June 2014. Then write the headline you would put on a slide, and the note you would add under it.
questions.hint: One CTE with category, year, month and line total. Then conditional SUMs: whole years for the first change, months 1 to 6 for the second.

questions.title: Does the pattern hold in every product?
questions.story: Before you present "deals close at a higher win rate in quarter-end months", check the trend inside each segment. For each product, among closed deals, return the win rate in quarter-end months (March, June, September, December), the win rate in the other months (percent, 1 decimal) and a column called quarter_end_higher with 'Yes' or 'No'. Is the overall pattern a Simpson's paradox?
questions.hint: Two conditional rates per product in a CTE, then a CASE WHEN that compares them.

questions.title: BookMe: canvas and issue tree for +30%
questions.story:
BookMe is a travel booking platform that mostly sells bus tickets. After the strategy talk, leadership says next year's focus is to grow revenue by at least 30% against this year. The market for this kind of business grows about 15% a year. You are interviewing as a data analyst for BookMe.

Part 1: draw a Business Model Canvas that shows how BookMe earns money.
Part 2: build an issue tree for the question "How do we grow BookMe revenue by at least 30% next year?"

Write both as text here. Indented lines are fine for the tree. The tree must be MECE and at least 3 levels deep.
questions.hint: Think of every leaf as a query you could run. The SQL questions in this lesson show how: a branch has to reach every row ("Which split covers every deal?"), a branch that comes back flat is still a finding ("Is the March jump the same in every office?"), and canvas boxes get numbers from data ("AdventureWorks channels in numbers"). For the volume-versus-price split at the top of your tree, see the case on customers versus order size.
guide: Do the arithmetic first. The market gives +15%, the target is +30%, so BookMe has to grow 1.30 / 1.15 = 1.13 times faster than the market, about 13% more than the market alone. Write one line on how much of the +30% comes from the market and how much BookMe must win from competitors.

Canvas: fill the boxes you can state from what you know about the business: customer segments, value proposition, channels, revenue streams, key partners, costs. Put a question mark on every box you are guessing and write the question you would ask.

Start the tree with a formula, because a maths split is MECE by construction: Revenue = tickets sold x revenue per ticket. Then split each part again: tickets sold = buyers x tickets per buyer, revenue per ticket = ticket price x take rate.
Where the formula runs out, split by a business cut instead, such as new vs returning buyers, or by route or by channel. Use one kind of split per level.
Test every level twice. Overlap: can one item sit in two branches? Full cover: does every item land in a branch? Rename or remove the branches that fail.
End each branch with a leaf you can measure and name the metric. "Improve marketing" is not a leaf. "New buyers from paid search per month" is.
State your assumptions and one source for each (annual report, news article, market note). There is no single right tree.

links.why: Check that a branch reaches every row
Test one branch of a tree with data
Put numbers into canvas boxes

links.why: The volume-versus-price split on real data

links.case: Revenue by country: which country do we mean?

questions.title: ShopSmart: a different tree for +45%
questions.story:
ShopSmart is an eCommerce platform that sells home goods and furniture. After a strategy talk, leadership sets a goal to grow revenue by at least 45% against last year. The eCommerce market is projected to grow 20% a year.

Part 1: draw a Business Model Canvas for ShopSmart.
Part 2: build an issue tree for "How do we grow ShopSmart revenue by at least 45% next year?"
Part 3: put your tree next to your BookMe tree (or imagine one) and write two lines on what changes and why.
questions.hint: Start with the definition, as in "Two win rates": decide what counts as a customer and a repeat order before you split. Then use the same data habits as the AdventureWorks cases: separate new from returning customers, and check whether average order value moved before blaming customer behaviour.
guide: Arithmetic first: 1.45 / 1.20 = 1.21, so ShopSmart has to beat the market by about 21%. Compare this with BookMe's 13%. Which goal is harder, and what does that say about where the growth must come from?

Canvas: think about what makes furniture different. High price, few purchases per customer, bulky delivery, returns, and long research before buying. Let those facts show up in the boxes (channels, costs, key activities).

Use a different top split from the BookMe tree on purpose. Try customers first: new customers vs returning customers, then orders and order value inside each. Or use the funnel: visitors x conversion rate x order value.
Go at least three levels deep. Give each level one kind of split (a formula, then a segment, then a driver).
Run the two MECE tests on every level and fix the failing branches. Check that the branches add up to the whole target, not to a part of it.
Finish each branch with a metric you could compute. For furniture, ask whether repeat purchase is a realistic branch or a branch to drop, and say why.
For Part 3, write which parts of the two trees are the same (revenue formula) and which are specific to the business.

links.why: Fix the metric definition before the tree
Channel split with real numbers

links.case: 2013 revenue: new customers or returning ones?
links.why: The new versus returning branch on data

links.case: Average order value fell 75%. Did customers spend less?
links.why: When the order-value branch hides a mix change

links.why: Check that a split covers every sale

questions.title: Break a question into five parts
questions.story:
Three product questions were written as one long sentence. For each one, fill in the five parts of an analytics question: Problem and context, What/How/Why, Metrics, Action, Goal. In Metrics, list the key metric and its sub-metrics. Write the three answers as three short blocks or a table.

a. "Our platform is experiencing a decline in new user retention rates after 1-2 weeks on the platform. How can we determine if implementing a personalized onboarding process improves new user retention rates so that we can achieve a 25% increase in active users by the end of Q3 2025?"

b. "We are facing increased competition in our market segment. How can we analyze user engagement metrics to determine if our new loyalty program increases customer loyalty, aiming for a 30% growth in repeat purchases by the end of 2024?"

c. "Customer feedback indicates dissatisfaction with our delivery times. How can we evaluate the impact of optimizing our delivery logistics on customer satisfaction scores to achieve a 20% increase in positive feedback by the end of 2025?"
questions.hint: The metric line is where most answers go wrong, so build it first. "Two win rates" shows how one word can mean two different numbers. "Split won value into input metrics" shows how a key metric breaks into sub-metrics you can compute. For the duration metric in (c), remember that an average of days can mislead; the retention-style questions (a) and (b) have a data example in the cases listed below.
guide: Find the Goal first. It is the number and the date at the end of each question. Copy it as written.
Problem and context is what is happening now, before the question mark. Add the baseline you would need to measure it (for example, which period the drop is measured over).
What/How/Why: what you want to learn, how you would test it, and why it matters. Write it as a comparison: group A against group B, over one period.
Action is the change the business makes if the answer is yes. If the question never names one, write the action you would propose and say that the question left it out.

Metrics: one key metric with a written definition (what is counted, out of whom, over which period). Then two to four sub-metrics. A sub-metric is an input that explains the key metric, a segment cut, or a guardrail that must not get worse.
Check the key metric with one question: could two analysts run it and get the same number? If not, a part of the definition is missing.

links.why: Write the definition into the metric line
Break a key metric into sub-metrics

links.case: How long does a sale take, and does it depend on the product?
links.why: A duration metric (for question c)

links.case: The 2018 promotion: did it bring members who stay?
links.why: A retention metric (for questions a and b)

questions.title: North Star Metric for seven companies
questions.story:
Define a North Star Metric (NSM) for each of these companies, from your own research: Canva, Pinterest, Twitter, Shopify, TikTok, Coursera, Shopee.

For each one write: the NSM as one sentence with a unit and a period, one line on why it shows value to the customer, and one input metric a team could move. Then pick two companies and add the One Metric That Matters (OMTM) you would give a team in its first year.
questions.hint: Practise the move on data you can query. "Split won value into input metrics" turns one output into inputs with a multiplication that must add up. "Does the detail follow the total?" checks that the parts really explain the whole. The cases on revenue growth do the same split on AdventureWorks and on a web store, and ask which input did the work.
guide: Start from the value the customer gets. Ask which single action shows that the customer got what they came for.

Write the NSM as count + object + period. The course example for a bill-pay service is "monthly active paying users". Revenue is the weakest NSM: it measures what customers pay, and an NSM should measure what they get.
Test each candidate with four questions. Does it show value delivered? Does revenue follow it a few months later? Can a team move it? Can you compute it from data the company has?

Platforms with two sides (Shopee, Shopify) should count a completed exchange, not a visit. Content products (Pinterest, TikTok, Twitter, Canva, Coursera) should count an engaged or finished action, since an open alone says little.
Split the NSM with maths to find input metrics, for example NSM = active users x actions per active user. Pick one input per company.
OMTM is different from the NSM. It is the one number a team focuses on for a period, chosen by product stage (for example new users early, churn later).
Several answers are valid. Marks go for the four tests and your reasoning.

links.why: Split one output into input metrics
Check that your inputs explain the whole

links.why: Which input moved the output

questions.title: MeStyle: from objective to issue tree and metrics
questions.story:
MeStyle is a mid-sized online fashion shop founded in 2021. By 2024 sales were falling, many carts were abandoned and the team could not explain customer behaviour. Management wants to use e-commerce analytics to (1) reduce cart abandonment and (2) understand customer behaviour and preferences so marketing works better. You are the new data analyst.

1. Draw a Business Model Canvas for MeStyle: how does it make money?
2. Pick at least one of the two objectives and write the analytics question in the five parts (Problem and context, What/How/Why, Metrics, Action, Goal). Assume a numeric goal, for example +20% customer retention year on year.
3. Build an issue tree for your question: MECE, at least 3 levels.
4. List the metrics and dimensions you would analyse from the tree and say why you picked each.
questions.hint: Every step of this task has a SQL question in this lesson: check that detail follows the total, count how many groups each dimension returns, run the 80/20 check, find where a change came from, and estimate an effect with a what-if. The web-store funnel case is the closest picture of your tree.
guide: Canvas first, and keep it specific to online fashion: revenue from product sales, costs of goods, shipping, returns and ads, and the channels where customers arrive. Mark the boxes you are guessing.
Pick one objective. Write the five-part question with a numeric goal and say that the goal is your assumption.

Use the funnel as the backbone of the tree if you chose cart abandonment: abandonment rate = 1 - orders / carts created, and a session leaves at exactly one last stage (cart, checkout, payment, confirmation). That makes the stages MECE.
Under each stage, split by cause family: price or shipping surprise, friction (forms, payment methods), trust, technical errors, no intent to buy. Keep one kind of split per level.
For each leaf pick a metric and the dimensions you will cut it by (device, traffic source, new vs returning, category, day). For each dimension write the decision it informs.
Size the dimensions before you slice. A dimension with 2 values reads at a glance, one with 2,000 needs a Top N. Start where the mass is (the 80/20 check) and report a flat result as a finding.
Finish with a what-if: if abandonment fell from X% to Y%, how many more orders and how much revenue? Label X and Y as assumptions.

links.why: Check that each tree level adds up to the level above
Size every dimension before you slice
Find where the mass is
Find which branch drove the change
Size the prize with a what-if

links.case: Where do visitors drop out on the way to an order?
links.why: A funnel on web store data

links.case: Do 20% of products really bring 80% of revenue?
links.why: The 80/20 check on real data

questions.title: Name the bias: five judgement calls
questions.story:
Name the bias in each situation using the seven from the lesson (confirmation, framing, availability, sampling, survivorship, outliers, Simpson's paradox). For each one give the evidence in one line and the fix.

a. A company reviews a marketing campaign. The team only highlights the sales increase in the demographic that matched what they expected.
b. A hiring manager favours candidates from a prestigious university and ignores equally qualified candidates from lesser-known schools.
c. A company reports that 85% of customers are satisfied and calls it overwhelmingly positive, without saying that few customers answered the survey.
d. A research team stresses the findings that support its hypothesis about consumer preferences and dismisses the data that shows a different trend.
e. A rival launches a product. The company reads only its negative reviews, assumes it will fail, and ignores its strong first sales.
questions.hint: Two SQL questions in this lesson show the same biases in data. "Two headlines for 2014" is framing: one dataset, two honest headlines. "Winners only: who is missing?" shows what a one-sided view leaves out. Work out how you would show each situation with numbers, then name it.
guide: Read each situation and ask the red-flag question of the three cognitive biases. Confirmation: did anyone look for evidence against the idea? Framing: would the decision change if the same fact were worded the other way? Availability: is this common, or only memorable?
Write the bias, then one line of evidence taken from the text: which words in the situation show it.
If two biases fit, name the main one and mention the second. Say which family each belongs to (cognitive or statistical).
The fix must be an action: test the opposite, show absolute and relative numbers, use base rates and the full period.
Check your fix against the six questions before you share (alternatives, comparisons, base rate, sample, missing, shape).

links.why: Framing: one dataset, two headlines
What a one-sided view leaves out

links.case: Delivery time fell by almost half. Is that still the headline?
links.why: Framing: which two points does a headline compare?

questions.title: Name the bias: five numbers that mislead
questions.story:
Name the bias in each situation using the statistical ones (sampling, survivorship, outliers, Simpson's paradox). For each give the evidence in one line and say what query or comparison you would run to show it.

a. A company runs a satisfaction survey, but only users who opened the email can answer.
b. An investment firm judges its portfolio by looking only at funds that are still active.
c. A sales team sees a few reps far above everyone else and concludes that sales training works.
d. A company compares two regions. Region A has higher total sales, but per person Region B does better.
e. A business studies the demographics of its most loyal customers and concludes that marketing should target only that group.
questions.hint: Four SQL questions in this lesson run these comparisons on real tables: a winners-only average against all closed deals, a mean against a median, a total against a rate, and a pattern that is checked inside every product. Find the one that matches each situation and copy its comparison.
guide: Use the red-flag question of each statistical bias. Sampling: who is in my sample and who is not? Survivorship: who is missing from this data? Outliers: does the median tell the same story as the mean? Simpson's paradox: does the trend hold in every segment?
Name the group that is missing or the number that is stretched, and use that as your evidence line.
For each situation write the comparison that would show the problem: a second group, a rate instead of a total, a median next to a mean, a count of those who left.
If a situation fits two biases, name the main one and note the other.
Say what you would report instead, in one sentence a manager can use.

links.why: Survivorship: who is missing?
Outliers: mean or median?
Total or rate: who leads?
Simpson's paradox: does the pattern hold in every segment?

questions.title: Turn an analysis into a 5 to 7 slide deck
questions.story:
Take an analysis you already have results for. In class, use the analysis your mentor shares. For practice in the Lab, use one case from the Case Studies tab, or your answer to "Two headlines for 2014".

Pick one or two topics from it (overall trend, growth, product, place, customer) and write a deck of 5 to 7 slides for a manager who has three minutes. For each slide write: the slide number, the title as a full-sentence takeaway with a number and a period, the chart you would show, and one line of message. Finish with a bias check: which of the seven biases could undermine your main claim, and what you did about it.
questions.hint: Your SQL answers already hold the slides. "Two headlines for 2014" is a framing choice for slide 2. "Top 3 categories and Other" is a chart choice for slides 4 and 5. "Does the pattern hold in every product?" is the bias check for slide 7. Pick one finding and build the deck around it.
guide: Choose one or two topics. Five to seven slides cannot carry more.
Write the answer first, in one sentence. Then the two or three arguments that support it. Then the data under each argument. This is the Pyramid Principle, and it is slide 2.

A deck that works: 1 title with the question and the answer, 2 summary (answer, key points, what you ask for), 3 context and metric definitions (situation, complication, question, answer), 4 and 5 one insight each, 6 recommendation with the size of the prize and the next steps, 7 optional: risks and the bias check.
Write every title as a takeaway: what happened, the number and the period. "Online is 88% of orders but 27% of revenue" is a title. "Orders by channel" is a label.
One chart per slide and one message per chart. Use a rate when the groups differ in size, and Top 3 plus Other when a chart has many categories.
Finish with the six questions: alternatives, comparisons, base rate, sample, missing, shape. Write one line for each that applies.
Read the deck aloud. If it takes more than three minutes, cut a slide.

links.why: Two headlines: a framing choice
A readable chart for many categories
The bias check slide

links.case: Deals close better at quarter end. Real pressure or a reporting habit?
links.why: A full analysis to present

links.case: Delivery time fell by almost half. Is that still the headline?
links.why: A headline to defend, with a bias check
